You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Meta: Can Muse Turn AI Into Its Next Profit Engine?

TEXT:
Muse Has Suddenly Changed the Trading Narrative Around Meta
Meta has emerged as one of the strongest-performing mega-cap tech stocks in September, with the key catalyst being the September 8 launch of its personal AI agent, Muse. The app reached roughly 2.8 million downloads within just 12 days and quickly climbed to the top of the U.S. App Store rankings. Since Muse was launched, Meta shares have gained more than 20%, including an 11.3% single-day jump on September 21, showing how quickly investors have started reassessing Meta’s position in consumer AI.
That shift is particularly important. Over the past two years, discussions around Meta’s AI strategy have focused largely on massive data-center spending, GPU purchases, and improvements in advertising recommendations. Muse gives investors a much more direct commercialization path: Meta may be able to turn AI from a back-end productivity and recommendation tool into a standalone consumer-facing business.
3.6 Billion Users Could Be Muse’s Biggest Competitive Advantage
Muse can already handle tasks such as email management, shopping, travel bookings, and certain transaction-related activities. Meta currently offers a free version alongside $20 and $100 monthly subscription tiers. Mark Zuckerberg has also indicated that Meta eventually plans to charge small transaction fees when Muse completes purchases or other commercial activities.
Jefferies estimates that if Muse eventually reaches one billion users and converts around 3% of them into paying subscribers, annual revenue could reach roughly $10.8 billion by 2027.
The more important advantage, however, is Meta’s distribution network. As of the second quarter, Meta’s family of apps had reached 3.6 billion daily active users. If Muse is gradually integrated into Instagram, WhatsApp, Facebook, and Meta’s hardware ecosystem, it can reach an enormous installed user base without having to build a completely new distribution channel from scratch.
The latest Meta Connect event reinforced this direction. Meta announced deeper integration of Muse into its AI glasses, allowing users to perform tasks such as bookings, shopping, and exercise planning through voice commands. The company also introduced the $349 Ray-Ban Meta Audio and other next-generation smart-glasses products. This suggests Muse is increasingly being positioned as a unified AI interface spanning software, hardware, and real-world interactions.
Massive AI Spending Now Needs New Revenue Validation
Muse is especially important because Meta’s AI investment cycle has become increasingly aggressive. In the second quarter, revenue reached $60.8 billion, up 28% year over year. Ad impressions increased 14%, while the average price per ad rose 12%, showing that the core advertising business remains strong. At the same time, quarterly capital expenditure reached $31.1 billion, while Meta expects full-year 2026 capex of between $130 billion and $145 billion.
This means the market is gradually shifting its focus from whether AI can improve advertising efficiency to whether Meta’s enormous AI infrastructure investment can generate entirely new revenue streams.
Muse offers that possibility. Subscription revenue, transaction fees, shopping-related commissions, and future business services could all become additional growth engines beyond advertising.
The risks are also clear. Muse’s user growth has been rapid, but there is still limited evidence regarding paid conversion, long-term retention, and actual transaction volume. Amazon has already restricted Muse’s access to its shopping platform, showing that AI agents may face resistance once they begin controlling valuable consumer purchase flows. Meta has also tested human-assisted support for some Muse phone-based tasks, suggesting that agent reliability in more complex real-world activities still has room to improve.
Meta Enters a High-Level Consolidation Phase Near $740
On the technical side, META has entered a period of high-level consolidation following its sharp September 21 rally. The stock closed at $744.10 on September 23, up 1.02%, after reaching an intraday high of $763.90 and setting a new 52-week high.
In the near term, the $760–765 area has become the first major breakout zone, while $730–740 is the nearest support range. If the stock pulls back further, the $700 area will become an important level for assessing whether the broader breakout structure remains intact.
Muse has already triggered the first round of expectation-driven rerating. The next stage will depend on whether Meta can produce stronger evidence around user growth, paid conversion, and transaction activity. If Muse can gradually translate engagement into revenue, Meta’s valuation framework could continue expanding from “advertising platform plus AI spending” toward “advertising platform plus consumer AI gateway.”
